canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is solving a math problem, often a grade-school or benchmark-style word problem, and returning a correct final numerical or symbolic answer. Many definitions also allow or expect intermediate calculations or chain-of-thought traces before that answer, and some papers describe success as generating equations, symbolic expressions, or full step-by-step derivations. Papers also make this link explicit: several claim causal relationships from Chain of thought to mathematical problem solving, while only isolated papers make similar causal claims from Instruction following or Self-correction.

Variants. The prevailing variants are math word problem solving and arithmetic problem solving, with papers covering everyday word problems, arithmetic expressions, algebra, geometry, probability, and competition-style questions. Smaller strands study long-context or low-resource-language settings, tool-using setups where models invoke code or arithmetic tools, and visual settings that require interpreting diagrams, graphs, or equations in images. Other papers carve out more specialized variants, including operations research formulation from text, polynomial root-finding, nonlinear ODE solving, and symbolic versus visual equation solving; in Can Vision-Language Models Solve Visual Math Equations?, one definition contrasts equations 'presented in textual form within images' with cases where the model must 'infer coefficients by counting icons'.

Space of elicitation and scores. Across papers, it is measured by 35 instruments, most often GSM8K and MATH, followed by MATH-500, SVAMP, and AIME 2024. These are mostly benchmark datasets or evaluation suites spanning grade-school word problems, competition math, and more specialized arithmetic or algebra tasks, with some broader dialogue-style evaluations that include a math component. Scoring usually turns on correctness of the final answer, though papers also mention solve rate, extracting numerical answers from generated solutions, F1 on GSM8K, and whether generated symbolic expressions are functionally correct.

What it is taken as evidence of. Across papers, it is linked to 7 constructs, and the links do not converge on a single construct. The most common links are that mathematical problem solving is related to Reasoning, Mathematical reasoning, Chain-of-thought reasoning, Commonsense reasoning, and Logical reasoning, mostly as related links rather than direct measurement claims. Two additional construct links appear only as causal claims directed toward mathematical problem solving, so papers do not present a single agreed construct that this behavior reflects.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the dominant framing is solving a math problem, often a grade-school or benchmark-style word problem, and returning a correct final numerical or symbolic answer. Many definitions also allow or expect intermediate calculations or chain-of-thought traces before that answer, and some papers describe success as generating equations, symbolic expressions, or full step-by-step derivations. Papers also make this link explicit: several claim causal relationships from Chain of thought to mathematical problem solving, while only isolated papers make similar causal claims from Instruction following or Self-correction.

characterization_sections.label: Variants.
characterization_sections.text: The prevailing variants are math word problem solving and arithmetic problem solving, with papers covering everyday word problems, arithmetic expressions, algebra, geometry, probability, and competition-style questions. Smaller strands study long-context or low-resource-language settings, tool-using setups where models invoke code or arithmetic tools, and visual settings that require interpreting diagrams, graphs, or equations in images. Other papers carve out more specialized variants, including operations research formulation from text, polynomial root-finding, nonlinear ODE solving, and symbolic versus visual equation solving; in Can Vision-Language Models Solve Visual Math Equations?, one definition contrasts equations 'presented in textual form within images' with cases where the model must 'infer coefficients by counting icons'.

characterization_sections.label: Space of elicitation and scores.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, it is measured by 35 instruments, most often GSM8K and MATH, followed by MATH-500, SVAMP, and AIME 2024. These are mostly benchmark datasets or evaluation suites spanning grade-school word problems, competition math, and more specialized arithmetic or algebra tasks, with some broader dialogue-style evaluations that include a math component. Scoring usually turns on correctness of the final answer, though papers also mention solve rate, extracting numerical answers from generated solutions, F1 on GSM8K, and whether generated symbolic expressions are functionally correct.

characterization_sections.label: What it is taken as evidence of.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, it is linked to 7 constructs, and the links do not converge on a single construct. The most common links are that mathematical problem solving is related to Reasoning, Mathematical reasoning, Chain-of-thought reasoning, Commonsense reasoning, and Logical reasoning, mostly as related links rather than direct measurement claims. Two additional construct links appear only as causal claims directed toward mathematical problem solving, so papers do not present a single agreed construct that this behavior reflects.
